audience.audienceType: Discrete and process manufacturers, auto-component and engineering suppliers, and MSME factories

props.title: Fewer breakdowns, fewer rejects, plans that hold
props.lede: AI agents for manufacturers that watch machine data for early signs of failure, record quality checks as they happen, re-plan when an order changes and reorder material before the line stops. They read from the ERP, PLCs and maintenance logs you already have.

intro.title: What does Exyconn build for manufacturing?
intro.definition: is a set of agents that reads machine, quality and stock data from the shop floor and turns it into maintenance alerts, inspection records, production plans and purchase requests, so supervisors and planners act on today's data instead of last week's. Exyconn designs, builds and runs these agents on your ERP, your PLC or SCADA data, your maintenance records and the WhatsApp groups your shift teams already use. Engineers and quality heads still make the calls on stopping a line or releasing a lot.

benefits.title: Why manufacturers are doing this now

items.text: Many machines already log temperatures, cycle times and alarms through their PLCs. Most of that data is never looked at.
An unplanned breakdown on a bottleneck machine costs the whole shift's output, not just the repair.
Customers and auditors ask for traceable inspection records, and paper check sheets are slow to search.
Order books change weekly. Plans built once a month in a spreadsheet can't keep up.
Experienced supervisors are retiring, and what they know about each machine is rarely written down.

demo.title: whatsapp · maintenance desk
demo.caption: The agent spots a rising temperature trend on a press, alerts the maintenance engineer and helps book a stop between shifts.

messages.text: Suresh, the hydraulic oil temperature on Press 4 has been climbing for three days and is now well above its usual range at full load. Last time this pattern showed, the cooler fan motor was failing.
Bracket part BR-220 for the Pune customer, 2,400 pieces left on the order, due Friday. Press 6 can run the same die but is free only after 4pm.
Ok. Book a 1 hour stop at shift change and move the rest to Press 6

Done. Work order raised for the cooler fan with the spare from stores, the planner has been told, and the production plan now shows BR-220 on Press 6 from 4pm. I'll check temperatures again after the repair.

props.label: The reality
props.title: Where a plant's hours actually go
props.lede: Talk to a plant head about a bad week and the same causes come up. Few of them are a surprise in hindsight.

items.title: Breakdowns nobody saw coming
items.text: Bearings, motors and hydraulics usually give warning signs in vibration, temperature or current. Without someone watching the trend, the first sign anyone notices is the machine stopping.

items.title: Quality checks on paper
items.text: In-process inspections are written on check sheets and typed up later. When a customer complaint arrives, tracing the lot, shift and operator takes days.

items.title: Plans rebuilt in Excel
items.text: A rush order, a missing die or an absent operator means the planner rebuilds the schedule by hand, and the shop floor hears about it late.

items.title: Lines waiting for material
items.text: Stock in the ERP and stock on the rack disagree. Shortages surface when the line stops, and purchase orders go out on urgent rates.

items.title: Safety and compliance records scattered
items.text: Permits, near-miss reports, PPE checks and statutory inspection dates live in registers and files, and are pulled together only before an audit.

items.title: OEE calculated after the fact
items.text: Downtime reasons, cycle times and rejects are logged per shift by hand, so the OEE figure is a week old and the real reasons for losses are guessed.

offerings.title: Six jobs AI takes off your team's plate

items.title: Predictive maintenance
items.text: Reads vibration, temperature, current and alarm data from PLCs, SCADA or add-on sensors, spots trends that have preceded past failures and raises a work order in your maintenance system before the breakdown.

items.title: Quality inspection
items.text: Captures inspection results and defect photos from the line on a phone or tablet, checks them against the control plan, and alerts the quality engineer when a measurement drifts. Release and rejection decisions stay with your QC team.

items.title: Production planning
items.text: Builds and re-plans the schedule from open sales orders, machine capacity, tooling and material availability in the ERP, and shares each shift's plan with supervisors for approval.

items.title: Inventory and procurement
items.text: Compares the plan's material needs with stock and open POs, raises purchase requisitions for approval, chases suppliers on delivery dates and records receipts and GRNs against the order.

items.title: Safety and compliance
items.text: Runs daily safety checklists and work permits in chat, logs near-misses with photos, and reminds owners before statutory inspections, calibrations and certificate renewals fall due.

items.title: OEE and output dashboards
items.text: Calculates availability, performance and quality per machine and shift from machine signals and operator inputs, and answers questions like "why was line 2 slow on Tuesday night" in plain language.

props.label: A day with it running
props.title: One day at an auto-component plant running three shifts
props.lede: Follow a normal Wednesday. Each moment lights the part of the plant the agent is working on.

moments.title: The night shift, in numbers
moments.text: OEE per machine, output against plan and the top three downtime reasons from the night shift are on the plant head's phone before the morning meeting.

moments.title: The safety walk is logged
moments.text: The shift in-charge completes the checklist in chat. A blocked fire exit near the paint shop is photographed and assigned to facilities with a deadline.

moments.title: A dimension starts drifting
moments.text: Bore diameters on a CNC cell are trending towards the upper limit. The quality engineer is alerted with the last 20 readings and stops the cell for a tool change.

moments.title: A rush order is fitted in
moments.text: A customer pulls an order forward by a week. The agent proposes a revised plan that moves two jobs, and the planner approves it before the second shift starts.

moments.title: Steel ordered before the shortage
moments.text: The revised plan needs more coil than is in stock or on order. A purchase requisition is raised for approval and the usual supplier is asked to confirm a date.

moments.title: A spindle sounds wrong
moments.text: Vibration on a grinding machine has crossed the level seen before its last bearing failure. A work order is raised for the next planned stop and the spare is reserved.

items.question: Will this replace our maintenance, quality or planning staff?
items.answer: No. The agents watch data and handle the paperwork so your engineers can act sooner. Stopping a line, releasing or rejecting a lot and approving purchases remain decisions for named people.

items.question: Our machines are old. Can we still do predictive maintenance?
items.answer: Often, yes. Machines with PLCs usually expose some data already. For older machines, add-on vibration, temperature or current sensors can be fitted. We start with the machines whose breakdowns cost you most and only add hardware where it pays for itself.

items.question: Which ERP and shop-floor systems do you connect to?
items.answer: We work with ERPs and accounting systems such as SAP, Microsoft Dynamics, Oracle and Tally, along with MES, SCADA historians and maintenance software, through their APIs, databases or exports. In the first weeks we confirm what each system exposes and agree read and write access with your IT team.

items.question: Is our production data safe?
items.answer: Machine and production data stays in your network or an environment set up for your company. Shop-floor connections are read-only unless agreed, access is role-based and every action is logged. Personal data of workers is handled under India's DPDP Act 2023 or the GDPR where it applies.

items.question: Can operators use it in their own language?
items.answer: Yes. Operators and supervisors can send updates and ask questions by voice or text in Hindi, English and other Indian languages, and get replies in the same language.

items.question: How much does it cost?
items.answer: It depends on the number of machines, lines and systems, and whether sensors are needed. Most plants start with one line. Tell us about your plant and we'll send a fixed quote for that first phase.
